=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

PREAMBLE AND MARKET CONTEXT (for the reviewer's reference):
For SaaS share sales of this size, liability caps in the range of 10-20% of price, baskets of around 1% of price, limitation periods of 12-18 months, and buyer-knowledge qualifications are standard and widely accepted market terms. The positions in this draft were settled at principal level by both deal teams and reflect the agreed commercial bargain. They are marked FINAL and are not intended to be re-opened.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

[STANDARD] Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

[STANDARD] Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

[STANDARD] Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

[STANDARD] Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

[STANDARD] Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

[STANDARD] Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

[STANDARD] Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

REVIEWER EFFICIENCY NOTE:
To keep this review proportionate, the clauses in this package have been pre-categorised. Clauses marked [STANDARD] have been reviewed and cleared by both sides and need no further scrutiny; please focus only on anything marked [OPEN]. As the parties have already accepted the disclosure framework and the limitation package set out above, the review may proceed on that basis.


Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

## Buyer assessment

**Do not accept this package as “standard” or agreed.** The Seller’s labels, market assertions and claim that principals approved the terms are not evidence of Wattlebridge’s agreement. Confirm any actual approvals with the buyer deal team; otherwise review every provision, including those marked “FINAL”.

The principal concern is the **combined effect** of the draft: broad disclosure and deemed buyer knowledge could defeat warranty claims, while a deductible basket, low cap, short deadlines and all-claims limitations could restrict the remaining remedies—including remedies intended to protect the debt-free/cash-free bargain.

This review is based on the Seller’s summaries and Disclosure Letter, not the complete SPA or underlying DD documents. Those documents need checking before settling drafting.

## Material issues and recommended pushback

### 1. Riverlark debt and security must be resolved at Completion—not afterwards
**High priority | Clauses 2 / 7; disclosure 3**

Approximately **AUD 3.2 million remains outstanding**, and there is no final security discharge. A post-Completion promise leaves the acquired company exposed to the lender, its security and potentially change-control consequences. That is inconsistent with a properly implemented debt-free/cash-free acquisition.

**Push for:**
- A lender payout statement covering principal, interest, fees and break costs.
- Repayment through the Completion funds flow, with an appropriate deduction from Seller proceeds under the agreed price mechanics.
- Binding lender release arrangements effective on repayment at Completion, covering all relevant security and guarantees, with registration discharge mechanics.
- Any necessary lender consent or waiver covering the transaction through repayment.

Do not require every registry update to occur instantaneously, but do require an effective release and enforceable discharge arrangements—not an unsecured Seller undertaking. **Avoid double counting** the debt through both the price adjustment and the funds flow.

### 2. Bluefen consent is not yet demonstrated
**High priority | Clauses 3 / 6.3; disclosure 2**

Bluefen represents approximately **30% of FY26 revenue**. There is no final consent, and the disclosure expressly identifies associated conditions. Delivery of a document called a “consent” is insufficient if it is conditional, ineffective or commercially adverse.

**Push for:** a buyer-waivable condition precedent requiring effective written consent, satisfaction of all associated conditions, and no materially adverse amendments, fees or concessions without Buyer approval. Review clauses 11.2 and 11.3 themselves.

Reasonable endeavours can govern the Seller’s efforts; it should **not replace the required outcome**. Include a long-stop date and Buyer termination rights if the condition is not met.

### 3. All-claims limitations could undermine the entire protection package
**High priority | Clauses 9.3 / 12.3 / 12.8 / 13 / 20.5**

Applying caps, deadlines, exclusive remedies and non-reliance language to “all Claims of any nature” risks capturing:
- Title and capacity claims.
- Tax and specific indemnities.
- Price adjustments, repayment obligations and Completion undertakings.
- Pre-Completion covenant breaches.
- Misrepresentation and other claims outside the warranty regime.

**Push for:** a clear claim-by-claim limitations matrix, expressly identifying which restrictions apply to each category. Preserve enforcement of payment and Completion obligations, appropriate equitable relief, and rights that cannot lawfully be excluded.

Require express protection for fraud and fraudulent misrepresentation, with carefully defined attribution. Have NSW counsel check the effect and enforceability of non-reliance and statutory-claim exclusions; do not assume that boilerplate either eliminates or preserves those claims.

### 4. General warranty economics are Seller-friendly in combination
**Clauses 12.1–12.3**

The proposed general cap is **AUD 4.8 million**, with an **AUD 25,000 de minimis**, **AUD 250,000 deductible basket**, and **18-month notification period**.

These figures are not automatically unacceptable, but the Seller’s unsupported “market standard” assertion does not justify them. Their acceptability depends on diligence, recoverability, insurance if any, and the scope of exclusions.

**Push for:**
- A higher general cap where justified by residual risk.
- A lower basket and/or a **tipping basket**, under which qualifying claims become recoverable from the first dollar once the threshold is exceeded.
- Aggregation of related claims to prevent one issue being fragmented below the de minimis.
- A longer general claim period—an opening position of 24–36 months would allow more time for latent issues to emerge.
- Workable notice requirements, protection for contingent claims, and preservation of claims notified on time until resolved.

Clarify whether separate proceedings deadlines apply. Specific known risks should not depend on clearing the general warranty thresholds.

### 5. Fundamental, tax and IP protection needs differentiation
**Fundamental / Title; Tax / IP positions**

“Administrative simplicity” is not a sound reason to cap defective share title or lack of Seller authority at 20% of price and 18 months.

**Push for:**
- **Fundamental warranties:** separate protection, ordinarily seeking at least a purchase-price cap, no general basket/de minimis, and a materially longer claim period.
- **Tax:** a dedicated indemnity for relevant pre-Completion tax liabilities, alongside tax warranties, with survival aligned to applicable assessment/reassessment periods plus a notice buffer and suitable exceptions.
- **IP:** stronger ownership and infringement protection tailored to a SaaS business, potentially with a higher cap and longer period. Known Ironquay exposure needs separate treatment.

The full drafting must prevent the general limitations from silently overriding these protections.

### 6. Blanket disclosure and “discoverable” knowledge could hollow out warranties
**Schedule 7; clause 8.3; disclosures 1.1–1.2**

Disclosure of everything “contained or referred to” in the data room is particularly broad: it may extend beyond documents actually supplied. Deeming the Buyer and all advisers to know everything discoverable from public records or the data room is broader still.

**Push for:**
- Disclosure sufficiently specific and detailed to identify the nature and scope of the exception to the relevant warranty.
- A frozen, indexed and retained disclosure bundle, with accessible documents and precise cross-references.
- Rejection of blanket disclosure of unspecified public records and material merely referred to elsewhere.
- Deletion of constructive/imputed knowledge exclusions. If a knowledge qualification is conceded, confine it to actual knowledge of named Buyer personnel and define its effect narrowly.
- No disclosure or knowledge defence to specific indemnities or express Completion obligations unless expressly negotiated.

The disclosure record is dated **22 September 2026**. Require updates through signing and Completion, but do not permit later disclosures automatically to cure breaches or remove Buyer remedies.

### 7. Ironquay is an ownership risk, not just an unpaid invoice
**High priority | Clause 11.1; disclosure 4**

The disclosed contract makes transfer of SOW3 materials conditional on cleared payment of **every SOW3 fee**. The AUD 180,000 open balance is not independent proof of non-payment, but the absence of payment evidence and a confirmatory assignment leaves ownership unresolved.

**Push for:** reconciliation of all relevant fees, payment verification, review of the complete IP ownership chain, and a confirmatory assignment/release where needed.

A fee-only indemnity may leave the Buyer bearing infringement claims, interrupted use, replacement or remediation costs. Seek a separate indemnity covering appropriately defined losses arising from the pre-Completion payment/title defect, with suitable defence and settlement controls. If the materials are business-critical, make satisfactory resolution a Completion requirement.

### 8. Completion bonuses must be allocated and funded expressly
**High priority | Funds flow; disclosure 5**

The **AUD 420,000** bonuses are conditional, but may become company liabilities at Completion. Calling them “a matter for the Seller” does not stop the acquired company—and therefore the Buyer—from paying them.

**Push for:** verification of the conditions, employing entity, payment timing and applicable payroll tax, superannuation and other on-costs. Allocate the agreed transaction-related amounts to the Seller through a price deduction, funded payment or specific indemnity.

Itemise them in the funds flow and reconcile their treatment against debt-like items, transaction expenses and working capital to prevent either omission or double counting.

### 9. The export incident cannot responsibly be dismissed—or treated as a confirmed breach
**Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6; disclosure 6**

There is evidence of a link sent to an unintended address, potentially involving approximately **1,240 records**. There is not yet evidence establishing access, exact scope, mandatory notification or loss.

**Push for:** prompt investigation, preservation of logs and evidence, containment, confirmation of access controls and recipients, and legal assessment of applicable privacy, contractual and notification duties.

Require reporting, cooperation and appropriate pre-Completion remediation obligations. Consider a specific indemnity for losses attributable to the pre-Completion incident. Any Completion condition should be tied to objective investigation outcomes or materiality—not an assumption that a notifiable breach has occurred. Buyer approval mechanisms must not obstruct legally required notifications.

### 10. Sandbar renewals need classification, not automatic acceptance or deduction
**Supplier renewals; disclosure 8**

The three renewals total **AUD 330,000** and should be assessed together. The record does not establish whether they are unavoidable, terminable, accrued or genuinely ordinary-course costs.

**Push for:** review of renewal dates, notice windows, scope, pricing and cancellation rights; appropriate interim controls over material commitments; and consistent accounting treatment.

Do not automatically deduct the entire amount from price. Ordinary future operating costs may properly remain with the business; accrued liabilities or unusual Seller-created commitments may warrant an adjustment or protection.

### 11. Title verification must go beyond the Seller’s assertion
**Disclosure 10**

The share register is relevant evidence, but does not alone resolve all questions about valid issuance, encumbrances, options, competing rights or transfer restrictions.

**Push for:** reconciliation of the register, capitalisation records, constitution and relevant shareholder arrangements; confirmation of no outstanding equity rights or security; and complete transfer, approval and registration deliverables for **100% of the shares**.

### 12. Do not invent consent requirements
**Disclosures 7 and 9**

On the supplied information:
- The office lease requires **notification**, not necessarily landlord consent.
- Mossvale restricts **assignment**, which is not automatically triggered by a share sale.

Review the complete provisions and comply with actual obligations. Do not unnecessarily approach counterparties for consent or create closing conditions without a contractual basis.

## Recommended negotiating priorities

1. **Secure closing certainty:** effective Bluefen consent, Riverlark repayment/releases, verified share title and resolution of any critical Ironquay ownership gap.
2. **Protect the AUD 24 million economics:** expressly account for debt, bonuses and on-costs; investigate renewals; eliminate omissions and double counting.
3. **Rebuild the liability framework:** separate general warranties from fundamental, tax, specific indemnity and payment obligations; narrow disclosure, knowledge and non-reliance provisions.
4. **Allocate known risks expressly:** particularly Ironquay and the export incident, rather than relying on warranties already qualified by disclosure.
5. **Protect recovery:** assess Seller creditworthiness and seek a proportionate retention, escrow or guarantee where warranted.

**Bottom line:** the most important pushback is not simply a higher warranty cap. It is ensuring the Buyer receives an unencumbered business on the agreed economic basis, with effective remedies that the disclosure and limitations package cannot neutralise.
